# Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Pericardial diseases > Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade*

[Original Article Link](/library/uh0pff)

---

## Summary

<u>Pericardial effusion</u> is the acute or chronic accumulation of fluid in the <u>pericardial space</u> (between the parietal and the <u>visceral pericardium</u>) and is often associated with a variety of underlying disorders. The fluid can be either bloody (e.g., following <u>aortic dissection</u>) or serous (usually <u>idiopathic</u>). As the <u>pericardium</u> is rather stiff, the capacity of the <u>pericardial space</u> is limited. In chronic effusion, the <u>pericardium</u> can stretch to a certain degree, accommodating slightly more fluid. In the acute setting, however, the added volume quickly exceeds the maximum capacity of the <u>pericardial space</u>. In both cases, the end result is often <u>cardiac tamponade</u>: compression of the <u>heart</u> that can lead to a life-threatening reduction in <u>cardiac output</u>. <u>Pericardial effusion</u> is initially asymptomatic, but <u>cardiac tamponade</u> has a distinct clinical presentation, including <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, jugular venous congestion, and <u>pulsus paradoxus</u>. <u>Echocardiography</u> is the most important diagnostic procedure and usually reveals an <u>anechoic</u> <u>pericardial space</u>. Treatment depends on hemodynamic stability: unstable patients require quick <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u>, through either <u>pericardiocentesis</u> or <u>surgery</u>, whereas in stable patients, treatment focuses on the underlying disease.

---

## Etiology

* Hemopericardium: accumulation of blood in <u>pericardial space</u>

* Cardiac wall rupture (e.g., complication of <u>myocardial infarction</u>)

* Chest trauma (traumatic <u>cardiac tamponade</u>)

* <u>Aortic dissection</u>

* Cardiac <u>surgery</u> (e.g., <u>heart valve</u> <u>surgery</u>, coronary <u>bypass surgery</u>)

* Serous or serosanguinous <u>pericardial effusion</u> [[2]](/library/NP0-UT)

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* <u>Acute pericarditis</u> (especially viral, but also fungal, tuberculous or bacterial)

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* <u>Postpericardiotomy syndrome</u>

* <u>Uremia</u>

* Autoimmune disorders

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Right heart failure</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>Cardiac tamponade</u>: <u>pericardial</u> fluid collection (e.g., bloody or serous) → ↑ pressure in the <u>pericardial space</u> → compression of the <u>heart</u> (especially of the <u>right ventricle</u> due to its thinner wall) → interventricular septum shift toward the <u>left ventricle</u> chamber → ↓ systemic <u>venous return</u> (<u>preload</u>) → ↓ ventricular <u>diastolic</u> filling → ↓ <u>stroke volume</u> (and venous congestion) → ↓ <u>cardiac output</u> and equal end-<u>diastolic</u> pressures in all 4 chambers




![Cardiac tamponade](media/ywuxhgrd3nqtg8x3y5ax8v39.jpg)

Cardiac tamponade

---

## Clinical features

### <u>Pericardial effusion</u> [[3]](/library/RBYl07)




* Initially asymptomatic in most cases

* <u>Shortness of breath</u>, especially when lying down (<u>orthopnea</u>)

* Retrosternal <u>chest pain</u>

* Can cause compressive symptoms

* <u>Hoarseness</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>

* <u>Dysphagia</u>

* <u>Hiccups</u>

* Apical impulse is difficult to locate or nonpalpable.

* Ewart sign: dullness to percussion at the base of the left <u>lung</u> with increased <u>vocal fremitus</u> and <u>bronchial breathing</u> due the compression of <u>lung parenchyma</u> by the <u>pericardial effusion</u> [[4]](/library/pBYLb7)





### Tamponade [[3]](/library/RBYl07)




* Beck triad  

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* Muffled <u>heart sounds</u>

* Distended neck <u>veins</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>, <u>pulsus paradoxus</u>

* <u>Pallor</u>, cold sweats

* <u>Left ventricular failure</u>

* <u>Symptoms of right heart failure</u>

* <u>Obstructive shock</u>, <u>cardiac arrest</u> (presenting as <u>pulseless electrical activity</u>) [[1]](/library/qBYCb7)





![Cardiac tamponade](media/ywuxhgrd3nqtg8x3y5ax8v39.jpg)

Cardiac tamponade

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Unstable patients with suspected tamponade: Do not delay treatment for extensive diagnostic workup; proceed directly with <u>management of cardiac tamponade</u>.

* In all other patients, confirm the diagnosis with <u>echocardiography</u> (either <u>TTE</u>, <u>FAST</u>, or <u>focused cardiac ultrasound</u>).

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> and analysis of the <u>pericardial</u> fluid can be used in the investigation of the underlying etiology.





> [!WARNING]
> In unstable patients and those in <u>cardiac arrest</u> with suspected tamponade, <u>pericardiocentesis</u> should not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation.




### <u>Echocardiography</u>




* Indication: diagnosis and monitoring of all patients with suspected <u>pericardial effusion</u> and/or tamponade [[5]](/library/9mcN310)

* Procedure: : <u>TTE</u> (<u>gold standard</u>), <u>FAST</u>, or <u>focused cardiac ultrasound</u> (<u>FoCUS</u>)

* Allows for the detection of: [[6]](/library/fbbkGH)

* Small effusions of 25–50 mL during ventricular <u>systole</u>

* Effusions of > 50 mL throughout the <u>cardiac cycle</u>

* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u>

* Ultrasound findings supportive of pericardial effusion: Can be identified using <u>POCUS</u> (See “Subxiphoid view" of the “<u>FAST scan</u>.”)

* <u>Anechoic</u> space between the <u>pericardium</u> and <u>epicardium</u>   [[7]](/library/rBYfX7)

* < 10 mm: small effusion ∼ 300 mL

* 10–20 mm: moderate effusion ∼ 500 mL

* > 20 mm: large effusion > 700 mL

* Hemorrhagic or <u>purulent</u> effusions may be echogenic.

* Echocardiographic findings supportive of cardiac tamponade [[7]](/library/rBYfX7)[[8]](/library/Jmcsg10)

* Chamber collapse 

* Early signs: collapse of the <u>right atrium</u> during <u>systole</u>, collapse of the <u>right ventricle</u> during early <u>diastole</u>

* Later: collapse of the <u>left atrium</u>  [[7]](/library/rBYfX7)

* Rare: collapse of the <u>left ventricle</u>

* Swinging motion of the <u>heart</u> 

* Inspiration: decrease in LV filling

* Exhalation: increase in LV filling and decrease in RV filling

* Blood flow changes during inspiration

* <u>Aortic valve</u> and <u>mitral valve</u>: decrease

* <u>Pulmonary valve</u> and <u>tricuspid valve</u>: increase

* <u>Hepatic vein</u> and <u>inferior vena cava</u> <u>plethora</u> (See “<u>IVC ultrasound</u>.”)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Echocardiography</u> is a quick and safe diagnostic tool for detecting <u>pericardial effusions</u> and <u>pericardial tamponade</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Epicardial fat can be mistaken for <u>pericardial</u> fluid on <u>echocardiography</u>. However, unlike fluid, it tends to be brighter, moves along with the <u>myocardium</u>, and does not collect in <u>dependent regions</u>. [[8]](/library/Jmcsg10)

### <u>ECG</u>




* Indication

* All patients with suspected <u>pericardial effusion</u>

* Used to rule out an <u>ischemic</u> cause

* Findings in <u>pericardial effusion</u>

* Normal in smaller effusions

* Low <u>voltage</u> complexes and <u>electrical alternans</u> in larger effusions

* Findings in <u>cardiac tamponade</u> [[4]](/library/pBYLb7)

* <u>Sinus tachycardia</u>

* <u>Low voltage QRS complexes</u>

* Electrical alternans: consecutive <u>QRS complexes</u> that alternate in height due to the swinging motion of the <u>heart</u> when surrounded by large amounts of <u>pericardial</u> fluid

* <u>Pulseless electrical activity</u> (<u>PEA</u>) in <u>cardiac arrest</u>  [[9]](/library/UVbbFs)

### Imaging




* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: not required to diagnose <u>pericardial effusion</u> but often performed to exclude other <u>causes of dyspnea</u> [[10]](/library/fBYkZ7)[[11]](/library/mFYViI)

* PA view findings

* Normal in small effusions  [[12]](/library/35YSPp)

* Enlarged <u>cardiac silhouette</u> and clear <u>lungs</u> may be seen in moderate effusions.

* Water bottle sign: the radiographic sign of a large <u>pericardial effusion</u> in which the <u>cardiac silhouette</u> resembles a bottle

* <u>Lateral</u> view findings  

* Posterior inferior bulge sign: a change in the <u>silhouette of the heart</u> due to a <u>pericardial effusion</u> that collects in the <u>posterior</u>-inferior pericardiac recess and expands the <u>pericardium</u> [[13]](/library/E2b8jG)

* Pericardiac fat pad sign: a > 2 mm soft-tissue stripe between the epicardiac fat and the <u>anterior</u> <u>mediastinal</u> fat that may be visible <u>anterior</u> to the <u>heart</u> [[10]](/library/fBYkZ7)

* Further imaging [[7]](/library/rBYfX7)

* Indications: consider if small or <u>loculated</u> effusions are suspected or visualization via <u>TTE</u> is difficult

* Modalities include: <u>TEE</u>, <u>CMR</u>, CT





> [!TIP]
> ∼ 250 mL of <u>pericardial</u> fluid must be present before an effusion is visible on <u>chest x-ray</u>!

### Investigation of the underlying etiology




#### Pericardial fluid analysis [[14]](/library/XyY9d7)[[15]](/library/Tbb6GH)




* Indication: <u>pericardial effusion</u> of unclear etiology  [[15]](/library/Tbb6GH)

* Procedure: <u>Pericardial</u> fluid is obtained via <u>diagnostic pericardiocentesis</u>.

* Analysis [[15]](/library/Tbb6GH)

* Cell count

* ↑ <u>WBC</u> in infection

* ↑ <u>RBC</u> in hemorrhagic effusions

* <u>Gram stain</u> and culture

* <u>Cytology</u>

* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u>

* <u>Glucose</u> level: 60–80 mg/dL suggestive of malignant, parapneumonic, or tuberculous effusions, or <u>connective tissue disease</u>.

* Protein level: > 6.0 g/dL is associated with <u>purulent</u>, parapneumonic, and tuberculous effusions.

* <u>LDH</u>: Isolated <u>pericardial</u> fluid <u>LDH</u> elevation of > 300 units/dL suggests <u>malignant effusion</u>.

* Interpretation [[14]](/library/XyY9d7)

* There are no established biochemical thresholds for the classification of <u>pericardial effusions</u>.

* <u>Light criteria</u> can be used for interpretation.





| Interpretation of <u>pericardial</u> fluid samples |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fluid type | Appearance | <br>Etiology [[14]](/library/XyY9d7)<br> |
| <u>Transudate</u> | <br>* Clear<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Heart failure</u><br><br>* <u>Renal failure</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u><br><br>* Postradiotherapy<br><br><br> |
| <u>Exudate</u> | <br>* Cloudy, chylous<br><br> | <br><br>* Viral infection<br><br>* Inflammation<br><br>* <u>Malignancy</u><br><br>* Autoimmune disease<br><br>* <u>Chylopericardium</u><br><br><br> |
| Blood | <br>* Hemorrhagic<br><br> | <br><br>* Postcardiac <u>surgery</u><br><br>* Cardiac rupture<br><br>* <u>Aortic dissection</u><br><br>* <u>Tuberculosis</u> [[16]](/library/cyYaV7)<br><br>* <u>Malignancy</u>  [[16]](/library/cyYaV7)[[17]](/library/gbbFGH)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Purulent</u> [[18]](/library/1yY2V7)<br> | <br>* Thick, yellowish-white, cloudy<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Tuberculosis</u><br><br>* Bacterial infection<br><br><br> |

#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> and specific investigations [[11]](/library/mFYViI)




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u> if infection or inflammation

* <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>: elevated in infection or inflammation

* <u>Troponin</u>

* Can be slightly elevated in <u>pericarditis</u>

* Significantly elevated if there is associated <u>myocarditis</u>

* <u>Creatinine</u> <u>kinase</u>: elevated in <u>myocarditis</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: elevated <u>BUN</u> in <u>uremic pericarditis</u>





| Investigation of underlying etiology in <u>pericardial effusion</u> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Suspected etiology | Additional investigations to consider |
| <u>Acute pericarditis</u> | <br><br>* <u>Blood cultures</u><br><br>* If <u>tuberculosis</u> is suspected:<br><br>* Quanti-FERON <u>TB</u> assay<br><br>* <u>HIV test</u><br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u><br><br><br> |
| Uremic <u>pericardial effusion</u> | <br>* <u>Renal ultrasound</u><br><br> |
| Autoimmune disease | <br><br>* <u>ANA</u><br><br>* <u>Rheumatoid factor</u><br><br>* <u>ACPA</u><br><br>* <u>ANCA</u><br><br>* <u>Ferritin</u><br><br>* Imaging of other affected systems guided by reported symptoms<br><br><br> |
| <u>Malignancy</u> | <br><br>* Serum <u>calcium</u><br><br>* CT<br><br>* <u>PET scan</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Hypothyroidism</u> | <br><br>* <u>Thyroid function tests</u><br><br>* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Aortic dissection</u> | <br><br>* <u>D-dimer</u><br><br>* <u>CT angiography</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Postpericardiotomy syndrome</u> | <br><br>* <u>Blood cultures</u><br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u><br><br><br> |
| Trauma | <br><br>* <u>FAST scan</u><br><br>* <u>Trauma CT</u><br><br>* Additional <u>x-rays</u> as required<br><br><br> |

## Treatment

### Approach




* Unstable patients: Identify and <u>treat cardiac tamponade</u> urgently, if present.

* Stable patients

* Small <u>pericardial effusion</u>: <u>Conservative management</u> focusing on treating the underlying cause is usually sufficient.

* Large <u>pericardial effusion</u> causing symptoms or of uncertain etiology: Consider <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u>.

* All patients

* Treat the underlying cause, e.g., <u>manage acute heart failure</u>, <u>treat pericarditis</u>.

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>, e.g., <u>pain management</u>

* Disposition

* Consult cardiology urgently if <u>cardiac tamponade</u> is suspected (See “<u>Management of cardiac tamponade</u>”).

* Consult cardiothoracic <u>surgery</u> if surgical <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u> is indicated.

* If <u>pericardiocentesis</u> is performed, admit patients to hospital ward or observation unit for postprocedure monitoring, serial examination, and <u>pericardial fluid analysis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Surgical <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u> (e.g., <u>pericardiotomy</u> and <u>pericardiectomy</u>) is commonly performed for patients with traumatic, <u>purulent</u>, <u>loculated</u>, rapidly reaccumulating, or <u>malignant effusions</u>. [[11]](/library/mFYViI)




### Pericardial fluid drainage [[11]](/library/mFYViI)[[19]](/library/3wYSir)




* <u>Therapeutic pericardiocentesis</u> 

* Performed as a temporizing measure for <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients with <u>cardiac tamponade</u>

* Can relieve symptoms for large chronic or recurrent effusions

* Consider specialist referral for patients at high risk of reaccumulating <u>pericardial</u> fluid, e.g., for indwelling catheter or <u>pericardiectomy</u>

* See “<u>Pericardiocentesis</u>” for details.

* Pericardiotomy: the creation of an opening in the <u>pericardium</u> to allow continuous drainage of <u>pericardial</u> fluid (externally or into the <u>pleural space</u>) [[20]](/library/b6bHju)

* Surgical <u>pericardiotomy</u> (pericardial window): A surgical <u>incision</u> is made in the <u>pericardium</u>.  [[21]](/library/i5cJP10)

* Subxiphoid approach: can be done under <u>local anesthesia</u> at the bedside (e.g., emergency department or <u>ICU</u>) and allows external fluid drainage

* <u>Thoracotomy</u> approach: needs to be done in the operating room and allows drainage into the <u>pleural cavity</u>

* Percutaneous balloon <u>pericardiotomy</u>: A transthoracic needle introduces a balloon-tipped catheter into the <u>pericardial space</u> which is progressively dilated to create an opening wide enough for continuous drainage.

* Complications: The <u>mortality rate</u> varies from 8–19%, depending on the underlying etiology.  [[22]](/library/D2b1PG)

* <u>Pericardiectomy</u>: performed as definitive management for refractory <u>pericardial effusion</u>, effusion due to <u>constrictive pericarditis</u>, or <u>purulent pericarditis</u> [[12]](/library/35YSPp)





> [!WARNING]
> Treat <u>hemopericardium</u> due to <u>penetrating chest injury</u> surgically, e.g., with <u>pericardial window</u>, as soon as possible. Only consider <u>pericardiocentesis</u> as a temporizing measure if <u>surgery</u> is unavailable. [[23]](/library/ZyYZd7)

## Management of cardiac tamponade

> [!TIP]
> Acute <u>pericardial effusion</u> with <u>pericardial tamponade</u> is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate <u>pericardial</u> decompression.




### Rapid evaluation of unstable patients




<u>Cardiac tamponade</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, however, clinical features are poorly sensitive and the diagnosis is often confirmed retrospectively.  [[24]](/library/AmcRR10)




* Use <u>POCUS</u> to confirm the presence of a <u>pericardial effusion</u> (see “<u>Focused cardiac ultrasound</u>” or “<u>FAST</u>” for techniques).

* Suspect tamponade in patients with suggestive clinical features and/or bedside imaging findings.

* ≥ 70% of patients have ≥ 1 of the following:  [[24]](/library/AmcRR10)

* <u>Shortness of breath</u>

* ↑ <u>Heart rate</u>

* ↑ <u>JVP</u>

* <u>Pulsus paradoxus</u> (> 10–12 mm Hg)

* <u>Cardiac enlargement</u> on <u>CXR</u>

* <u>Beck's triad</u> is poorly sensitive for tamponade and it is very rare for all elements to be present  [[25]](/library/zmcrR10)

* < 50% of patients have <u>low voltage QRS complexes</u> on <u>ECG</u>. [[24]](/library/AmcRR10)

* Obtain an urgent bedside <u>echocardiogram</u> to evaluate for <u>echocardiographic findings supportive of cardiac tamponade</u>.

* Evaluate the need for immediate <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u>.

* Consult a cardiologist and/or cardiothoracic <u>surgeon</u> and consider using a scoring system to help determine when urgent <u>pericardiocentesis</u> is advised and when it can safely be deferred.  [[26]](/library/Bmcz310)[[27]](/library/ymcdR10)





> [!TIP]
> The most common underlying causes of <u>cardiac tamponade</u> are cardiac interventions (e.g., <u>PCI</u>, pacemaker implantation), <u>malignancy</u>, infectious or inflammatory <u>pericarditis</u>, mechanical <u>complications of MI</u>, and <u>aortic dissection</u>. [[28]](/library/xmcE310)




### <u>Cardiac arrest</u> due to suspected <u>cardiac tamponade</u>




See also “<u>Cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation</u>.”




* Nontraumatic <u>cardiac arrest</u> [[29]](/library/xCYE8r)

* Consider <u>POCUS in cardiac arrest</u> to confirm <u>pericardial effusion</u>.

* Pause <u>CPR</u> to perform immediate <u>pericardiocentesis</u> as soon as possible if <u>cardiac tamponade</u> is the suspected etiology. [[30]](/library/4uY3rI)[[31]](/library/HCYKtr)

* Blind <u>pericardiocentesis</u> can be performed using landmarks if no <u>ultrasound</u> guidance is available. . [[23]](/library/ZyYZd7)[[32]](/library/-BYDW7)

* <u>Traumatic cardiac arrest</u>

* Assume <u>pericardial</u> fluid seen on <u>FAST scan</u> is traumatic <u>hemopericardium</u>.

* Perform <u>emergency thoracotomy</u> with vertical <u>pericardiotomy</u>. [[23]](/library/ZyYZd7)





### Urgent <u>pericardial fluid drainage</u>




* Perform <u>pericardiocentesis</u> under <u>echocardiographic</u> (or <u>fluoroscopic</u>) guidance without delay in unstable patients unless indications for immediate <u>surgery</u> are present.  [[11]](/library/mFYViI)

* Do not delay immediate surgical management in patients with a low likelihood of successful <u>pericardiocentesis</u> due to immediate reaccumulation of <u>pericardial</u> fluid, for example in:  [[1]](/library/qBYCb7)[[26]](/library/Bmcz310)[[33]](/library/ayYQd7)

* <u>Type A aortic dissection</u>

* <u>Ventricular free wall rupture</u>

* Severe <u>blunt chest trauma</u> or <u>penetrating chest injury</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> <u>hemopericardium</u> refractory to percutaneous <u>hemostatic control</u>

* Refer for surgical management if <u>pericardiocentesis</u> is unsuccessful, e.g., due to difficult conditions  [[1]](/library/qBYCb7)[[8]](/library/Jmcsg10)[[33]](/library/ayYQd7)





### <u>Hemodynamic support</u>




Manage as <u>obstructive shock</u>.




* <u>Establish IV access</u> with two large-bore IV lines (peripheral or central).

* Cautious <u>fluid resuscitation</u> (only in <u>hypovolemic</u> patients)  [[34]](/library/H6YKmJ)

* <u>Inotropic</u> support: <u>dobutamine</u> DOSAGE   [[33]](/library/ayYQd7)

* Avoid <u>anesthetic agents</u> and <u>positive pressure ventilation</u>.  [[35]](/library/zVbrCs)

* See “<u>Hemodynamic compromise in mechanically ventilated patients</u>” for the management approach if <u>mechanical ventilation</u> is unavoidable.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Positive pressure ventilation</u> can lead to hemodynamic decompensation in patients with <u>cardiac tamponade</u>.




### Subsequent management




* Identify and treat the underlying cause: See “Investigation of underlying etiology” in “Diagnostics.”

* Monitor for complications and reaccumulation.

* <u>ICU</u> admission recommended [[12]](/library/35YSPp)

* Continuous <u>telemetry</u>

* Regular BP monitoring
